title: Education Getting Ready for College Firth, Jonathan
author: Firth, Jonathan
summary: Cognitive psychologist Jonathan Firth examines the well-documented difficulty many students face transitioning from high school to university, focusing on the mismatch between the learning strategies that served students well in secondary school and those that higher education actually requires. Drawing on research including a South African study by Nel and colleagues, Firth identifies specific demands that distinguish HE: more independent reading of complex material, greater emphasis on process and analysis over content recall, heavier note-taking during lectures, and more self-regulated learning with less structure. The article highlights the danger of 'strategy rigidity' -- students who, under stress, revert to familiar but suboptimal strategies like re-reading and highlighting rather than adopting the retrieval practice that research shows is more effective in demanding university contexts.
points: The most dangerous aspect of the high-school-to-university transition is strategy rigidity: under stress, students revert to re-reading and passive highlighting rather than adopting retrieval practice and elaborative interrogation that work at university level.

Research shows many students arrive at university relying on guidance that actively undermines their performance: re-reading, highlighting, and cramming before exams all show small or zero effect sizes compared to retrieval-based practice.

University-level reading demands differ qualitatively from high school reading: longer texts, complex argumentation, unfamiliar primary sources, and the expectation that students will synthesize across multiple sources rather than absorb a single textbook.

Schools can address the transition gap by explicitly teaching the 'why' behind study strategies -- explaining the memory research supporting spaced practice and retrieval -- giving students a conceptual framework to adapt when familiar scaffolding disappears.

Students who discuss learning strategies with knowledgeable adults before university transition are better equipped to self-regulate when the familiar structure of class schedules and teacher prompting is removed.
quotes: A couple of posts ago [ ] I discussed what university lecturers (should) know about learning, viewing this within the issue of SoTL -- the scholarship of teaching and learning in Higher Education settings. I thought I'd follow this up with an example that is of great interest to me: study skills, and how new students adapt to college and university contexts. This is of notable relevance to school practitioners as well as to lecturers (not to mention parents and the students themselves!).
